explanations.explanation: Paul, the man writing this letter, asks them to be "like-minded, having the same love, being united in spirit and purpose." That's a whole team pulling the same direction. Picture a tray of cookies that all agree on the oven temperature instead of each one demanding its own setting. That's the kind of unity he's after.

Bold is a fine thing to be, but it isn't what Paul asks for in this verse. He asks them to be "like-minded, having the same love, being united in spirit and purpose." The big ask here is about how they stand with each other. I think a lot of us would rather be fearless than agree with Brenda about the parking plan, but that's the ask.

explanations.answer: Generous with their money and time
explanations.explanation: Generosity is a good thing, but Paul doesn't mention it in verse 2. What he asks for is being "like-minded, having the same love, being united in spirit and purpose." He's asking them to be one in spirit and purpose. That's a different batch than giving, and he wants this one.

Joy it is. Paul writes, "then make my joy complete by being like-minded…" He says their unity would make his joy complete. A full cookie jar feels good, but Paul says what fills his is the believers living in unity.

Paul doesn't call it his mission here. He says, "then make my joy complete…" Being like-minded, with the same love and a united spirit and purpose, would fill up his joy. It's a heart word, not a job word.
Work is a decent guess, since Paul has plenty of it. But the word in verse 2 is "joy." He says, "then make my joy complete…" Their unity is what would round it out for him.

Paul says, "Do nothing out of selfish ambition or empty pride…" Those are two things to leave out of the mix. Selfish ambition is chasing the spotlight, and empty pride is puffing up with nothing inside. It's like a cookie that rises big in the oven and then drops flat when the door opens. All show, nothing underneath.

Worry is a real struggle for plenty of people, but Paul doesn't name it in verse 3. He says, "Do nothing out of selfish ambition or empty pride…" Those two are about how we treat each other. Tomorrow can handle itself for this card.
That pair sounds like it belongs in the verse, I'll give you that. But Paul's two are "selfish ambition or empty pride." Anger and jealousy aren't listed in verse 3. He stays with the two he names.

Paul writes, "…but in humility consider others more important than yourselves." Humility means the other person gets the spot at the front of the line in your mind. The other person gets the first cookie off the tray, and you wait for the second pan.

Fortunate is a nice word, but it's not the one Paul uses. He says, "…in humility consider others more important than yourselves." It's about how much weight we give the other person. Luck doesn't come into it.

Paul doesn't say experienced. He says, "…in humility consider others more important than yourselves." It doesn't depend on who has been around longest. Even the newest person in the bakery counts as more important, and that's the point.

Paul actually writes, "Each of you should look not only to your own interests, but also to the interests of others." He says "not only," which means your own interests still count. He's asking them to add the other person's interests to the list. So he never says to stop looking out for your own at all.

Right, it's false. Paul writes, "Each of you should look not only to your own interests, but also to the interests of others." Notice the words "not only." Your own interests stay on the list, and other people's get added right next to them, like a second pan going in the oven beside yours.

explanations.answer: Emptied Himself and took a servant's form
explanations.explanation: Paul says Christ Jesus "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness." The One existing in the form of God took the servant's place. Paul says to let this mind be in us. That's the whole pattern for the believers in Philippi.

explanations.answer: Took a throne and ruled the earth
explanations.explanation: That isn't what verse 7 says. Paul writes that Jesus "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness." There's no throne in this part. Paul shows Him going down first.

Verse 7 doesn't mention angels at all. Paul says Jesus "emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness." He came as a servant, and that's the point. It's a long way down from the form of God, and Paul wants us to see it.

Paul writes that He "humbled Himself and became obedient to death—even death on a cross." That's as low as the road goes. The Son who existed in the form of God went all the way down to a cross. Paul wants the believers in Philippians to see how far humility can reach.
Mountains show up all over the Bible, but not in this verse. Paul says Jesus became obedient "to death—even death on a cross." The word he chooses is cross. That's how low Paul says Jesus went.

A battlefield makes sense if you picture a hero's story, but verse 8 says something else. Paul writes, "became obedient to death—even death on a cross." The word is cross, not battlefield. Jesus didn't go down fighting. He went down obedient.

explanations.answer: Exalts Him to the highest place
explanations.explanation: Paul writes, "Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names." He humbled Himself all the way down, and God lifted Him all the way up. That little word "Therefore" is the hinge. I wish my own humility got results like that, but mostly mine gets me the last cookie crumb.

explanations.answer: Keeps Him hidden from the world
explanations.explanation: Verse 9 says the opposite. Paul writes, "Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names." Nothing about hiding. It's lifted up and out in the open.

explanations.answer: Sends Him back to serve again
explanations.explanation: That's not what Paul says here. He writes, "Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place and gave Him the name above all names." After the humbling comes the lifting. God puts Him in the highest place.

Paul says it's "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth…" That covers every place there is. Nobody and nowhere gets left out of the lineup. It's a big picture, and Paul painted it wide.

Paul really does say it, so this one is true. He writes, "that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth…" Three places are named, and every knee is included. It's a wide circle, and nobody gets left outside it.

Paul says, "and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father." Knees bow and tongues confess. The whole thing ends up giving glory to the Father. And it started with a Son who went low.

explanations.answer: That God the Father is holy
explanations.explanation: That sounds true, but it isn't what verse 11 says. Paul writes, "and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father." The confession is about Jesus, and it brings glory to the Father. Both are in the verse, just not the way this answer puts it.

Paul does mention the Spirit earlier, in verse 1, but not here. In verse 11 he writes, "and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father." That's the confession. It's about Jesus being Lord.

Paul writes, "…continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling." He says "continue," because they've always obeyed. And right after, in verse 13, he says it is God who works in them. So they're not doing it alone.

Paul doesn't tell them to wait for him. He says they've obeyed "not only in my presence, but now even more in my absence." He's not around, and he tells them to "continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling." That work goes on whether he's there or not.

Verse 12 doesn't say anything like that. Paul writes, "…continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling." It's about their own walk with God, not about shutting people out. Later in the passage he even pictures them shining in the world.

Paul writes, "For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose." God works in them in the wanting and in the doing. So the believers in Philippi don't have to supply the whole effort themselves. Honestly, I'd take that deal on any Monday.

It's actually true. Paul writes, "For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose." Both the wanting and the doing have God working in them. That makes verse 12 a lot less lonely.
Paul says, "Do everything without complaining or arguing…" Everything means everything. Even the batch that burns and the line that moves slow. It's a short sentence, but it covers a lot of ground.
Paul doesn't say that. He writes, "Do everything without complaining or arguing…" Nothing in the verse tells them to stop asking for help. He names two things to leave out, complaining and arguing.
Rest isn't what Paul is talking about in verse 14. He writes, "Do everything without complaining or arguing…" Those are the two things he wants gone. A good rest between batches is not on that list.

Paul says they are to be "blameless and pure, children of God without fault in a crooked and perverse generation, in which you shine as lights in the world…" Lights show up best where it's dark. A little bulb in a dark bakery gets noticed quick. That's what he pictures for the believers.
Paul doesn't call them strangers here. He says, "…in which you shine as lights in the world…" It's a picture of shining, not standing apart. The word he picks is lights.

Soldiers would make a strong picture, but it isn't the one in verse 15. Paul says, "…in which you shine as lights in the world…" Lights don't march or fight, they shine. That's the picture Paul chose.

explanations.answer: That he didn't run or labor in vain
explanations.explanation: Paul says it's "in order that I may boast on the day of Christ that I did not run or labor in vain." As they hold forth the word of life, his running and laboring will not have been for nothing. He says he'll boast about it on the day of Christ. That's a happy bit of boasting.

explanations.answer: That he was never once afraid
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say anything about never being afraid. He says, "in order that I may boast on the day of Christ that I did not run or labor in vain." His boast is about his work not being for nothing. Fear never comes up in the verse.

explanations.answer: That he finished every journey he planned
explanations.explanation: That's not in verse 16. Paul says, "in order that I may boast on the day of Christ that I did not run or labor in vain." He's talking about running and laboring, not about finishing plans. Nobody finishes every plan anyway. I still haven't finished my to-do list from the day I got my apron.

Paul writes, "I am glad and rejoice with all of you." Glad is the first word of the pair. He says it even while being poured out like a drink offering. That's a lot of gladness from a man in a hard spot.
Paul says, "I am glad and rejoice with all of you." Rejoicing is the second half of his pair. He does it with all of them, together. Joy tastes better shared, like a cookie broken in half.
Weary is an easy guess for someone being poured out. But verse 17 doesn't say it. Paul says, "I am glad and rejoice with all of you." Those are the two words he picks.

Grief would make sense to us, but it's not what Paul writes. He says, "I am glad and rejoice with all of you." Glad and rejoice are the two words in the verse. I think that's what makes it so surprising.
Paul doesn't say afraid in verse 17. He writes, "I am glad and rejoice with all of you." Those two words are his answer to being poured out. Fear isn't part of the verse.
Paul says the opposite. He writes, "So you too should be glad and rejoice with me." He asks them to be glad and rejoice, not to grieve. He wants them in the same joy he has.
That's right, it's false. Paul writes, "So you too should be glad and rejoice with me." He doesn't ask for grief. He invites them to share his gladness and rejoicing instead.
